Reading PEPs is a great way to get a concrete handle on the philosophy and thought processes that go into Python language features.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "unordered-list", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Poke around the Python stdlib itself and read the source. A lot of it is pure-Python, the rest is C. It's a good way to understand what features the language has, what it doesn't, and how you can code idiomatically. The stdlib itself has some good examples of style, and it serves as a good benchmark for Python code.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "unordered-list", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "Patch the stdlib.  ", "modifiers": {}}, {"text": "What is the GIL (Global Interpreter Lock)?", "modifiers": {"link": {"type": "question", "qid": 1883, "url": "https://www.quora.com/What-is-the-GIL-Global-Interpreter-Lock"}}}, {"text": " 
 ", "modifiers": {}}, {"text": "How does the Global Interpreter Lock affect performance in multi-threaded Python applications?", "modifiers": {"link": {"type": "question", "qid": 100887, "url": "https://www.quora.com/How-does-the-Global-Interpreter-Lock-affect-performance-in-multi-threaded-Python-applications"}}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "unordered-list", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "The last and ultimately "best" way in some sense to improve your knowledge of Python is to keep building increasingly non-trivial applications and getting your code reviewed and torn apart by someone more experienced than yourself.", "modifiers": {}}], "indent": 0, "quoted": false, "type": "unordered-list", "is_rtl": false}, {"spans": [{"text": "
